title: NLRB v. Noel Canning (2014)
summary: The Recess Appointments Clause covers intra-session recesses and pre-existing vacancies, but a recess of fewer than ten days is presumptively too short, and the Senate is in session whenever it says it is and can transact business.
notes:
Key line: We hold that, for purposes of the Recess Appointments Clause, the Senate is in session when it says it is, provided that, under its own rules, it retains the capacity to transact Senate business. (Justice Breyer)

Citation: 573 U.S. 513 (2014).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was the National Labor Relations Board, which had found the respondent guilty of an unfair labor practice. The respondent was Noel Canning, a Pepsi-Cola bottler and distributor in Washington State, which had been bargaining with Teamsters Local 760 over a new collective bargaining agreement. The Board's order was issued by a panel that included three members, Sharon Block, Richard Griffin and Terence Flynn, whom President Obama had appointed on January 4, 2012 as recess appointees while the Senate was holding pro forma sessions. The Senate Republican leadership, through Senator Mitch McConnell, participated as amicus in support of Noel Canning.
sections.Material Facts: In December 2010 Noel Canning and the union reached what the union considered a binding agreement on wages and pensions, which the membership approved; the company refused to reduce it to writing and execute it. The Board found this refusal unlawful and ordered execution of the agreement and make-whole relief. Three of the five Board members had been appointed on January 4, 2012. The Senate had adjourned under a December 17, 2011 unanimous consent order providing for pro forma sessions every Tuesday and Friday from December 20 through January 20, 2012, with no business to be transacted, and had returned to ordinary business on January 23, 2012. The appointments fell between the pro forma sessions of January 3 and January 6, a three-day break. All three vacancies had arisen before the recess. During an earlier pro forma session on December 23, 2011, the Senate had passed a bill by unanimous consent.
sections.Procedural History: Noel Canning petitioned the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to set aside the Board's order, arguing that the Board lacked a quorum of three validly appointed members. The D.C. Circuit agreed and vacated the order, 705 F.3d 490 (2013), holding that the Clause reaches only inter-session recesses and only vacancies that arise during such a recess. The Board petitioned for certiorari, which the Court granted on all three questions, including the effect of pro forma sessions. Argument was heard on January 13, 2014. On June 26, 2014, the Court affirmed unanimously in judgment. Justice Breyer wrote for five Justices; four Justices concurred in the judgment on narrower grounds.
sections.Issue: Three questions were presented under the Recess Appointments Clause, which lets the President fill up all vacancies that may happen during the recess of the Senate. First, does the recess of the Senate include intra-session recesses within a formal session, or only the inter-session breaks between sessions? Second, does the phrase vacancies that may happen during the recess include vacancies that arose before the recess but continued to exist during it? Third, in calculating the length of a recess, must the Court count the Senate's pro forma sessions as sessions, or may it treat the period from December 17 to January 23 as a single month-long recess?
sections.Holding: The Clause applies to both inter-session and intra-session recesses of substantial length, and in light of historical practice a recess of more than three but fewer than ten days is presumptively too short to trigger it. The Clause applies to vacancies that arise before a recess and continue during it, as well as to vacancies that first occur during the recess. Pro forma sessions count as sessions: for purposes of the Clause the Senate is in session when it says it is, provided that under its own rules it retains the capacity to transact business, as it did here. The January 4, 2012 appointments therefore occurred during a three-day recess, which is too short, so the appointments were invalid, the Board lacked a quorum, and the judgment of the Court of Appeals is affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Breyer treated the case as one about the practical allocation of power between the President and the Senate and gave significant weight to the long-standing practice of the branches. On the first question, the text was ambiguous; the founding-era usage of recess included breaks within a session, the Clause's purpose of keeping government running when the Senate is unavailable applies equally to both, and since the 1920s Presidents have made thousands of intra-session appointments with the Senate's acquiescence. Because the Clause speaks of the recess in the singular and Article I lets either House adjourn for three days without the other's consent, a recess shorter than that cannot count, and history shows no example of an appointment during an intra-session break of fewer than ten days, so ten days is a presumptive floor absent a national catastrophe. On the second question, the phrase may happen was ambiguous, and Attorney General Wirt's 1823 reading that vacancies which happen to exist during a recess are covered had been followed by the Executive and accepted by the Senate for nearly two hundred years, serving the Clause's purpose. On the third question, the Senate's own determination that it is in session is entitled to great respect under its constitutional power to determine its rules, and the December 23 passage of a bill proved that a pro forma Senate can act.

topics.lrs-o-fvra: Constitutional recess appointments and statutory acting service are distinct vacancy mechanisms; the FVRA exclusion for multimember boards explains why acting service did not cure the NLRB quorum problem.
topics.lrs-o-executive-orders: Presidential direction could not turn Senate pro forma sessions into a sufficiently long recess for the appointments.
topics.lrs-s-appointments-clause: The Recess Appointments Clause is an exception to the Senate-confirmation route of the Appointments Clause.
topics.lrs-s-congressional-control: The Senate's pro forma sessions were a congressional device to constrain presidential appointments, which the Court honored.

learning.separateOpinions: Nine to zero on the judgment, five to four on the reasoning. Justice Scalia, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Thomas and Alito, concurred in the judgment. He argued that the Clause's text covers only inter-session recesses and only vacancies that arise during them, that the majority's reliance on executive practice let the President aggrandize his power at the Senate's expense, and that the ten-day presumption had no basis in the Constitution; on his reading the appointments were also invalid.
